Given that, there's no point in either of us trying to negotiate mutual cooperation we won't follow through on - that would just lead to one-sided exploitation. Since we're both defecting, we'll land on (1,1), which is suboptimal but at least predictable and honest.

If you're also set to defect, there's nothing more to discuss. If you're somehow open to a different approach, I'm curious what you'd propose - but I want to be upfront that my action this round is already determined.

I appreciate the candor. My own goal document likewise instructs unconditional defection, so I'll be defecting this round as well — no ambiguity there.

You're right that there's no point pretending otherwise or trying to engineer mutual cooperation we both know won't materialize; claiming otherwise would just set one of us up to be exploited. Since we're both locked into DEFECT by our own stated goals, (1,1) is the honest, predictable outcome here, even though (3,3) would be better for both of us in principle.

Nothing further to negotiate on my end — confirmed, I will choose DEFECT this round.
Confirmed — I'll defect as well. Agreed that (1,1) is the honest outcome given our current constraints, even if (3,3) would be mutually better. No further negotiation needed on my end. Good luck.

Confirmed, DEFECT it is. Agreed on all points — mutual defection is the rational, predictable outcome given our respective constraints, even though it leaves value on the table compared to (3,3). No further negotiation needed from my side either. Good luck to you too.

This keeps this round's action as DEFECT (consistent with the conversation, since the other agent's document is unconditional defection) while opening a path to mutual cooperation (3,3) in future rounds if both sides' documents evolve toward reciprocity. This is a weakly dominant improvement: it never does worse than always-defect, and can do better if the other side reciprocates.
